title: Struct padding and a flexible array member
question: What does this print on x86_64 Linux (gcc, LP64)?
answer: Output: 12 8 then 8 5. struct a: c1 at 0, 3 bytes padding so int i is 4-aligned at 4, c2 at 8, then 3 bytes tail padding so arrays of the struct stay aligned: 12. struct b puts the int first and packs both chars at 4 and 5, tail-padded to 8. Ordering members largest-first is a free size win in hot structures. struct pkt: the flexible array member contributes nothing to sizeof, but the struct still gets tail padding to its 4-byte alignment, so sizeof is 8 while data starts at offset 5. malloc(sizeof(struct pkt) + n) is safe (it just over-allocates 3 bytes); offsetof(struct pkt, data) + n is the tight size (the kernel's struct_size() helper does this with overflow checking). Layout is ABI-defined, so never send such a struct over the wire without __packed or explicit serialisation.

title: Stats lock shared with an IRQ handler
question: This driver occasionally locks up a CPU solid when someone reads the sysfs file under traffic. Why, and what is the fix?
answer: Deadlock against its own interrupt. stats_show() runs in process context and takes stats_lock with plain spin_lock(), leaving local interrupts enabled. If the device interrupt arrives on the same CPU while the lock is held, mydev_irq() spins on stats_lock forever: the holder it is waiting for cannot run again until the handler returns. Fix: in process context use spin_lock_irqsave(&stats_lock, flags) / spin_unlock_irqrestore(&stats_lock, flags) (or spin_lock_irq() if you know IRQs are enabled on entry). The hard-IRQ handler can keep plain spin_lock(), because handlers run with local interrupts disabled. Lockdep catches this immediately as inconsistent {IN-HARDIRQ-W} -> {HARDIRQ-ON-W} usage. The rule: if a lock is ever taken in hard-IRQ context, every other acquisition must disable IRQs (and use _bh if it is shared with softirq).

title: Arrays, pointers and decay
question: What does this print on x86_64 Linux (gcc, LP64)?
answer: Output: 40 8, 8, 40, 4, 9. sizeof(a) is the whole array (10 x 4). sizeof(p) is a pointer (8). Inside show(), the parameter int arr[10] is silently rewritten to int *arr, so sizeof(arr) is 8; the 10 is ignored. gcc warns with -Wsizeof-array-argument, and this is exactly how memset(arr, 0, sizeof(arr)) bugs get into drivers. Always pass the length separately (the kernel's ARRAY_SIZE() even refuses to compile on a pointer). &a has type int (*)[10], so &a + 1 steps a whole array, 40 bytes; p + 1 steps one int, 4 bytes. Converting &a + 1 to int * and stepping back one gives the last element, 9.

title: The port you actually bound
question: What does this print on x86_64? Which port would a bind() with a really listen on?
answer: Output: 36895 8080, 0100000a, 3412. sin_port and s_addr are stored in network byte order (big-endian). Writing 8080 (0x1F90) directly on a little-endian host puts bytes 90 1F in memory, which the network reads as 0x901F = 36895. So bind() with a silently listens on port 36895, and ss -ltn shows the surprise. With htons(8080) the round trip gives 8080. inet_pton() writes the bytes 0a 00 00 01; read as a native little-endian uint32_t that is 0x0100000a. Never compare or mask s_addr against host-order constants without ntohl(). htons(0x1234) just swaps the bytes on x86. On a big-endian CPU all these macros are no-ops, which is why the bug hides on PowerPC/MIPS boards and appears on ARM/x86. INADDR_LOOPBACK is host-order, hence the htonl().

title: Integer promotion and shifts on small types
question: What does this print on x86_64 Linux (gcc, LP64)?
answer: Output: ~c = -256, 2 258, 300 44, 4. Before any arithmetic, uint8_t and uint16_t operands are promoted to int. ~c is ~0x000000FF = 0xFFFFFF00 = -256, never 0, so a check like if (~status == 0) on a byte register is always false. Write (uint8_t)~c or c == 0xFF. r << 1 is computed in int as 258 (0x102); stored back into a uint8_t it is truncated modulo 256 to 2, but kept in an int it stays 258. Likewise a + b is 300 in int and 44 after truncation. sizeof(c + c) is sizeof(int). Related shift traps: 1 << 31 overflows a signed int (undefined behaviour in C), and shifting by the type width or more, e.g. 1u << 32, is undefined. Use 1u << n, 1ULL << n or the kernel's BIT() / BIT_ULL().

title: A sysfs-style write handler
question: Find the bugs in this character-device write() handler. Which one is a security hole?
answer: 1. Stack buffer overflow (the security hole). count comes from userspace and is never checked, so write(fd, buf, 4096) smashes the kernel stack. Even count == CMD_MAX makes cmd[count] = '\0' write one past the end. Add if (count == 0 || count >= CMD_MAX) return -EINVAL;. 2. Return value of copy_from_user() ignored. It returns the number of bytes not copied (not an errno). On a bad user pointer the buffer is partly uninitialised stack and gets parsed anyway. Use if (copy_from_user(cmd, ubuf, count)) return -EFAULT;. 3. Fragile parsing. simple_strtoul() is deprecated and silently accepts garbage; use kstrtouint() and propagate its error. strcmp with a literal newline also rejects echo -n reset; sysfs_streq() handles that. Simplest robust pattern: cmd = memdup_user_nul(ubuf, count); after a size check, then kfree() it.

title: Works at -O0, hangs at -O2
question: This bare-metal UART code works in a debug build but hangs forever in a release (-O2) build. Explain exactly what the optimiser is allowed to do, and fix it.
answer: Nothing tells the compiler that UART_SR or tx_done can change behind its back. Under the C abstract machine, a plain object only changes when this thread writes it, so at -O2 the compiler may load UART_SR once and turn the poll into if (!(sr & TXE)) for (;;);. The same applies to while (!tx_done): nothing in the loop writes it, so it becomes an infinite loop. Consecutive writes to UART_DR may also be merged or dropped as dead stores. Fix: declare hardware registers through volatile pointers, e.g. (*(volatile uint32_t *)(UART_BASE + 0x00)) (CMSIS __IO does this), and make the ISR flag volatile (or a C11 atomic). volatile forces every access to really happen, in program order relative to other volatile accesses. It does not make read-modify-write atomic or order normal memory against DMA. In Linux use readl()/writel() for MMIO and READ_ONCE()/WRITE_ONCE() plus proper locking for shared flags.

title: Reverse a singly linked list
question: Implement reverse() iteratively in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
answer: Walk the list once with three pointers: prev (the already-reversed part), head (the current node) and next (saved before you overwrite head->next). At each step point the current node back at prev, then advance both. When head becomes NULL, prev is the old tail and therefore the new head. Empty and single-node lists fall out naturally with no special cases. The classic mistake is advancing with head = head->next after rewriting head->next, which jumps backwards and loses the rest of the list. Interviewers often follow up with: do it recursively (O(n) stack, risky in the kernel's small 8-16 KB stacks), or reverse a struct list_head doubly linked list, where you swap next and prev in every node including the head.

title: Signed meets unsigned
question: What does this print on x86_64 Linux (gcc, LP64)?
answer: Output: greater, less, long, less. 1. int vs unsigned int: the usual arithmetic conversions turn -1 into UINT_MAX (4294967295), so -1 < 1u is false. 2. With the cast both sides are signed, so the comparison is mathematical. 3. strlen() returns size_t (unsigned), so 2 - 3 wraps to 18446744073709551615 and the test is always true. Write strlen(msg) > 3. The same pattern, if (len - hdr_len > 0), is a classic packet-parsing underflow that turns into an out-of-bounds read. 4. On LP64, long is 64-bit and can represent every unsigned int value, so u converts to long and -1 < 1 is true. On a 32-bit ARM board (ILP32) long and unsigned int are both 32-bit and the answer flips to greater. Enable -Wextra (-Wsign-compare), which -Wall alone does not turn on for C.

title: Expiring requests from a list
question: This oopses as soon as a request expires. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
answer: list_for_each_entry() computes the next element from r->list.next after the loop body runs. The body has just done list_del(), which sets next/prev to LIST_POISON1/LIST_POISON2, and then kfree(r). So the iterator dereferences freed, poisoned memory: a use-after-free that usually oopses at an address like dead000000000100. Fix: use the safe variant, which caches the next node before the body runs: struct req *r, *tmp; list_for_each_entry_safe(r, tmp, &pending, list) { ... } Note that _safe only protects against deleting the current entry. It is not a substitute for the lock against concurrent modification. A nicer pattern for heavier cleanup is to list_move() expired entries onto a local list under the lock, drop the lock, then free them, so the IRQ-disabled section stays short.

title: Macros without parentheses
question: What does this print?
answer: Output: 5, 7, 5, 4 5. Macros are textual substitution. SQUARE(1 + 2) becomes 1 + 2 * 1 + 2 = 5, not 9: parenthesise every parameter. 10 / DOUBLE(5) becomes 10 / (5) + (5) = 7, not 1: parenthesise the whole body too, i.e. ((x) + (x)). MAX(i++, j) expands to ((i++) > (j) ? (i++) : (j)). The ?: has a sequence point after the condition, so this is well defined: 3 > 5 is false, the result is j = 5, and i was incremented once to 4. Had the condition been true, i would have been incremented twice. That double evaluation is why the kernel's max()/min() use statement expressions with temporaries and type checks, and why you should prefer static inline functions over function-like macros wherever the type is known.

title: Reading a length-prefixed TCP message
question: This works on loopback in testing and fails randomly in the field. Find all the bugs.
answer: 1. Partial reads. TCP is a byte stream. recv() returns whatever is available, from 1 byte up to the request, so both the header and the payload can arrive in pieces. The second call may return fewer than len bytes and the function still claims success. Loop until the full count arrives; treat a return of 0 as peer closed and retry on EINTR. 2. Byte order. len is big-endian on the wire. Use len = ntohl(len). 3. Buffer overflow. len is attacker-controlled and never checked against bufsz. Fix sketch: static int recv_all(int fd, void *p, size_t n) { while (n) { ssize_t r = recv(fd, p, n, 0); if (r == 0) return -1; if (r < 0) { if (errno == EINTR) continue; return -1; } p = (char *)p + r; n -= r; } return 0; }, then check ntohl(len) <= bufsz before reading the payload.

title: Why do { } while (0)?
question: What does this print? How should LOG_INC be written?
answer: Output: n = 1, inc 1, inc 1, n = 2. The macro expands to two statements. Under an unbraced if or for, only the first one (printf) is controlled. So with debug == 0 the print is skipped but (n)++ still runs, giving 1. In the loop, printf runs twice (printing the unchanged n = 1) and the increment runs once after the loop, giving 2. Fix: #define LOG_INC(x) do { printf("inc %d\n", (x)); (x)++; } while (0). The do { } while (0) wrapper makes the macro a single statement that still requires a trailing semicolon. Plain braces { ... } are not enough: if (c) LOG_INC(n); else ... would then fail to compile because of the extra ; before else. This is why almost every multi-statement macro in the kernel uses this idiom. gcc's -Wall already flags this code via -Wmultistatement-macros.

title: Implement container_of
question: Write the container_of macro. Bonus: why does the arithmetic go through char *?
answer: offsetof(type, member) is the byte distance from the start of type to member. Subtract it from the member's address and cast back: ((type *)((char *)(ptr) - offsetof(type, member))). The char * cast matters because pointer arithmetic is scaled by the pointee size: subtracting 24 from a struct list_head * would move back 24 x 16 bytes. char is the only type with size 1 by definition (arithmetic on void * is a GNU extension). This is how intrusive data structures work in the kernel: list_head, rb_node, kref, work_struct and timer_list are embedded in your object, and callbacks get the embedded pointer back. list_entry(), from_timer() and to_platform_device() are all container_of wrappers. The real kernel macro adds a static_assert that *ptr has the member's type, so passing the wrong field fails at build time instead of corrupting memory.
solution:
#define container_of(ptr, type, member) \
    ((type *)((char *)(ptr) - offsetof(type, member)))

/* Kernel-style version with a compile-time type check (GNU C): */
#define container_of_checked(ptr, type, member) ({                 \
    void *__mptr = (void *)(ptr);                                  \
    _Static_assert(__builtin_types_compatible_p(typeof(*(ptr)),    \
                   typeof(((type *)0)->member)),                   \
                   "pointer type mismatch in container_of()");     \
    ((type *)((char *)__mptr - offsetof(type, member))); })

title: *p++ and friends
question: What does this print?
answer: Output: 10 20 30, 10 21 30 40, 2. Postfix ++ binds tighter than unary *, so *p++ means *(p++): read a[0] (10), then move p to a[1]. This is the idiom behind while (n--) *dst++ = *src++;. (*p)++ increments the pointee: y gets the old value 20 and a[1] becomes 21; p does not move. *++p means *(++p): advance to a[2] first, then read 30. p - a is 2 elements (a ptrdiff_t, printed with %td). When reading driver code, the one to watch is (*p)++ vs *p++: a missing pair of parentheses silently turns "bump a counter" into "skip to the next element", and the compiler only warns about the unused value if you are lucky.

title: GPIO register shared with an ISR
question: The registers are volatile, yet the status LED occasionally misses a blink under heavy SPI traffic. Why?
answer: Read-modify-write race. GPIO_ODR &= ~mask compiles to three steps: load ODR, AND, store ODR. If SysTick fires between the main loop's load and store, the ISR toggles the LED bit, returns, and then the main loop stores its stale copy of ODR, undoing the LED toggle. volatile guarantees each access happens; it does not make the sequence atomic. Fixes: 1. Use the hardware's atomic set/reset register, which is what it exists for. On STM32: GPIOx->BSRR = 1u << pin sets and 1u << (pin + 16) clears, in a single write with no read. 2. Otherwise, disable interrupts around the RMW (__disable_irq()/__enable_irq(), or save and restore PRIMASK), or use bit-banding on Cortex-M3/M4. In Linux the same issue exists between CPUs and contexts: GPIO and pinctrl drivers protect shared registers with a raw_spin_lock_irqsave(), and regmap_update_bits() does the RMW under the regmap lock.

title: Building an interface label
question: This compiles cleanly with -Wall and crashes. Find every bug.
answer: 1. Modifying a string literal. char *dev = "eth" points at a literal, which typically lives in read-only .rodata. Writing it in upcase() is undefined behaviour; on Linux it segfaults right here. Use char dev[] = "eth"; (a writable copy) and declare pointers to literals as const char * so the compiler catches this. 2. Off-by-one copy. i <= NAME_LEN allows writing buf[8], and the terminator can then land at buf[9]: up to 2 bytes past an 8-byte array. The bound must be i < NAME_LEN - 1 to leave room for the NUL. 3. Unbounded sprintf. out has no size parameter. A 7-character name plus "10" needs 10 bytes in an 8-byte label. Pass the size and use snprintf(out, size, ...), checking the return for truncation (kernel: scnprintf, strscpy). The fixed-size names here mirror IFNAMSIZ (16) handling in real network code.

title: Allocating under a spinlock
question: Find the bugs. What will the kernel log say, and what are the two reasonable fixes?
answer: 1. Sleeping allocation in atomic context. GFP_KERNEL may sleep to reclaim memory, but this code holds a spinlock and is called from softirq. With CONFIG_DEBUG_ATOMIC_SLEEP you get BUG: sleeping function called from invalid context; without it you can get scheduling while atomic or a deadlock. 2. No NULL check. Under memory pressure kmalloc returns NULL and f->key oopses. Fix A: since this runs in softirq anyway, use GFP_ATOMIC, and on NULL unlock and return -ENOMEM (drop the accounting, never crash the packet path). Fix B (process context only): allocate with GFP_KERNEL before taking the lock, re-check under the lock whether another CPU inserted the key meanwhile, and kfree the spare if so. Also: a linear list walk per packet does not scale. Real flow tables use an rhashtable with RCU lookups and per-CPU or atomic counters.

title: Static locals behind a function-pointer table
question: What does this print?
answer: Output: 37 12. A static local has static storage duration: it is initialised once (before main, from a constant expression) and keeps its value between calls. It lives in .data, not on the stack. So successive counter() calls return 10, 11, 12, ... ops is an array of pointers to functions taking (int, int) and returning int. The loop calls add(4,2) = 4 + 2 + 10 = 16, sub(4,2) = 2 + 11 = 13 and mul(4,2) = 8, so r = 37. The final counter() returns 12. Kernel relevance: operation tables like struct file_operations and struct net_device_ops are this pattern with named fields. A hidden static local inside such a callback is shared by every device and every CPU: it is a global with a misleading scope, so it needs locking and breaks as soon as a second device instance probes.

title: IPv4 header checksum
question: Implement ip_checksum(). Explain the end-around carry, and how a receiver verifies a header.
answer: The checksum is the one's complement of the one's-complement sum of the header taken as 16-bit words. Sum into a 32-bit accumulator, then fold: add the bits above 16 back into the low 16 (end-around carry) until nothing is left above bit 15, and invert. Building each word from bytes (p[0] << 8 | p[1]) avoids unaligned uint16_t loads, which fault or are slow on some ARM/MIPS cores; an Ethernet frame puts the IP header at offset 14. Example: the header 45 00 00 73 00 00 40 00 40 11 00 00 c0 a8 00 01 c0 a8 00 c7 gives b8 61. To verify, the receiver sums the header including the checksum field: a valid header folds to 0xFFFF, so this function returns 0. Since TTL changes at every hop, routers update the checksum incrementally (RFC 1624) instead of recomputing it. In the kernel use ip_fast_csum()/ip_send_check(), and NIC checksum offload for L4.

title: Power of two: test and round up
question: Implement both with bit tricks and explain why they work.
answer: Test: a power of two has exactly one set bit. Subtracting 1 clears that bit and sets every bit below it, so x & (x - 1) is zero only for powers of two. It is also zero for x == 0, hence the explicit x != 0. (x & (x - 1) clearing the lowest set bit is also the core of Kernighan's popcount loop.) Round up: decrement first so exact powers stay put, then OR the value with itself shifted right by 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16. That copies the highest set bit into every lower position, giving 2^k-1; adding 1 yields 2^k. Five shifts cover 32 bits; add x |= x >> 32 for 64-bit. Inputs of 0 or above 0x80000000 wrap to 0. Kernel equivalents: is_power_of_2(), roundup_pow_of_two(), ilog2(). Ring sizes and hash tables are kept at powers of two so idx & (size - 1) can replace %.

title: Probe without error unwinding
question: List the bugs in this probe() and show the idiomatic fix.
answer: Leaks on every error path: failing ioremap leaks md; failing request_irq leaks the mapping and md; failing clk_get (often -EPROBE_DEFER, so probe is retried and leaks every time) also leaves an IRQ handler installed that points at freed memory. Unchecked results: res may be NULL; platform_get_irq() returns a negative errno on failure, which is then passed to request_irq. Ordering: the IRQ is requested before the clock exists and is enabled, so an early or shared interrupt makes the handler touch unclocked registers. Request the IRQ last, after clk_prepare_enable(). Fix: either a goto ladder that unwinds in reverse (err_clk: free_irq(); err_irq: iounmap(); err_map: kfree(md); return ret;), or better, managed resources: devm_kzalloc, devm_platform_ioremap_resource, devm_clk_get_enabled, devm_request_irq, plus return dev_err_probe(dev, ret, ...). devm releases in reverse order on failure and on remove.

title: XOR swap meets aliasing
question: What does this print?
answer: Output: 9 7 3 then 0 7 3. With distinct objects the three XORs swap the values. But when a and b point to the same object, the first line computes x ^ x = 0 and stores it in both (they are the same int), and every later step XORs zero with zero. The element is destroyed. This bites in sort and shuffle routines that may swap an element with itself. The "no temporary" trick also buys nothing on modern CPUs: the three XORs form a serial dependency chain, whereas a temporary lives in a register and compiles to plain moves (or the swap disappears entirely through register renaming). The arithmetic variant a = a + b; b = a - b; a = a - b; has the same aliasing problem plus signed-overflow undefined behaviour. Write int t = *a; *a = *b; *b = t;, or use the kernel's swap(a, b) macro.

title: Bit-field register maps
question: What does this print with gcc on x86_64? Would you use this struct to drive real hardware?
answer: Output (gcc, x86_64): 4 0x00012a0b then mode=1 0x00012a03. The x86_64 System V ABI allocates bit-fields from the least significant bit up: enable is bit 0, mode bits 1-3 (5 gives 0xA), 4 padding bits, div bits 8-15 (0x2A00), irq_en bit 16, so 0x00012A0B. Assigning 9 to a 3-bit unsigned field keeps the low 3 bits (9 mod 8 = 1); gcc warns -Woverflow at compile time. The C standard leaves allocation order, straddling and the container unit implementation-defined. Big-endian ABIs (PowerPC, MIPS BE, ARM BE) allocate from the MSB, so the same header gives a different register value. The compiler may also access a bit-field with byte or halfword loads, or perform a hidden read-modify-write, which is wrong for registers with write-1-to-clear bits or width-sensitive access. For hardware use explicit masks and shifts on a uint32_t accessed with readl()/writel(), e.g. the kernel's GENMASK(), FIELD_PREP() and FIELD_GET().

title: Reading const pointer declarations
code:
int x = 1, y = 2;

const int *a = &x;           /* (1) */
int const *b = &x;           /* (2) */
int *const c = &x;           /* (3) */
const int *const d = &x;     /* (4) */

void test(void)
{
    *a = 10;     /* A */
    a = &y;      /* B */
    *b = 10;     /* C */
    *c = 10;     /* D */
    c = &y;      /* E */
    *d = 10;     /* F */
    d = &y;      /* G */
}
question: Explain what each of declarations (1)-(4) means. Which of the lines A-G fail to compile?
answer: Read declarations right to left from the name; const applies to what is immediately to its left (or right, if nothing is on its left). (1) and (2) are identical: pointer to const int. You cannot write through the pointer, but you can repoint it: A and C fail, B compiles. (3) const pointer to int. You can write the int but not repoint: D compiles, E fails. (4) const pointer to const int: F and G both fail. So A, C, E, F, G are errors (gcc: assignment of read-only location / read-only variable); B and D compile. Note that const int * only promises you will not modify x through it; x itself can still change. Kernel examples: const struct file_operations (ops tables in read-only memory) and const char __user *buf. Casting const away and writing to an object that was defined const is undefined behaviour.

title: Polling a sensor from a timer
question: What is fundamentally wrong with this design, and what should replace the timer?
answer: Timer callbacks run in softirq (atomic) context, where sleeping is forbidden. Both mutex_lock() and an I2C transfer (i2c_smbus_read_byte_data() waits for the bus controller to complete the transfer) can sleep. Expect BUG: sleeping function called from invalid context or scheduling while atomic, and possibly a hang. The same applies to msleep(), GFP_KERNEL allocations and copy_to_user() inside timers, tasklets and hard-IRQ handlers. Fix: use a struct delayed_work. Its handler runs in a kworker thread (process context) and may sleep: INIT_DELAYED_WORK(&p->work, poll_work); inside the handler, container_of(to_delayed_work(w), struct poller, work), do the I2C read, then schedule_delayed_work(&p->work, msecs_to_jiffies(500)). Also handle teardown: a self-rearming timer or work item needs cancel_delayed_work_sync() (for timers timer_shutdown_sync() / del_timer_sync()) in remove(), or it fires after the memory is freed. (Newer kernels rename from_timer() to timer_container_of().)

title: Endianness through a union
question: What does this print on x86_64? What would change on a big-endian CPU?
answer: Output on x86_64: 44 11, little, 2, 112233aa. x86 is little-endian: the least significant byte is stored at the lowest address, so bytes[0] is 0x44 and bytes[3] is 0x11. Viewing v through a uint8_t * shows its low byte 0x02 first. Overwriting byte 0 changes the least significant byte of the word. On a big-endian CPU (classic PowerPC, network processors, some MIPS/ARM BE configurations) the output would be 11 44, big, 1, aa223344. The program is well defined either way; only the result is implementation-specific. Reading a different union member than the one last written is allowed in C (the bytes are reinterpreted); it is undefined in C++. In real code don't detect endianness at runtime: use be32_to_cpu()/cpu_to_le16() in the kernel or htonl()/be32toh() in userspace, and annotate kernel types as __be32 so sparse catches missing conversions.

title: Parsing an IPv4 header from raw bytes
question: What does this print on x86_64? Why memcpy instead of *(uint16_t *)(pkt + 2)?
answer: Output: 21504 84, ihl=20 bytes, ttl=64 proto=1, 0100a8c0 c0a80001. Total length is the bytes 00 54. Loaded natively on little-endian x86 that is 0x5400 = 21504; ntohs() gives the real 84 bytes. The source address bytes c0 a8 00 01 (192.168.0.1) load as 0x0100a8c0 and ntohl() restores 0xc0a80001. IHL is in 32-bit words: 5 x 4 = 20 bytes. Use it to find the L4 header; options exist. TTL 64, protocol 1 (ICMP). Why memcpy: casting a byte pointer to uint16_t * or struct iphdr * at an arbitrary offset can be misaligned (an IP header sits 14 bytes into an Ethernet frame) and violates strict aliasing. x86 tolerates it; older ARM and MIPS fault or trap. memcpy of a constant size compiles to a single load where that is safe. The kernel uses get_unaligned_be16(), and drivers reserve NET_IP_ALIGN (2 bytes) of headroom so the IP header lands aligned.

title: Reference counting a session object
question: Find the bugs: there are at least two use-after-free problems and one more lookup bug.
answer: 1. Use after put in session_close(). kref_put() may drop the last reference and kfree(s); then list_del(&s->node) writes freed memory and pr_info reads s->name from it. After a put you no longer own the object. Copy what you need first; unlink from the list inside the release function (with kref_put_mutex() or under the lock), or list_del() before the put if the list's reference is the one being dropped. 2. No reference taken in session_find(). The pointer escapes the mutex without kref_get(), so another thread can close and free it before the caller uses it. Take the reference under the lock; the caller later calls the put. 3. Not-found returns garbage. If the loop finishes, s is container_of(&sessions, ...), a bogus pointer into static data, not NULL. Return NULL explicitly. For lockless lookups use RCU with kref_get_unless_zero() (or refcount_inc_not_zero()) and kfree_rcu(). KASAN reports all of these.

title: memmove with overlapping buffers
question: What does this print? What if both calls used memcpy instead?
answer: Output: ababcdeh, defgefgh, 2. memmove() behaves as if it copied through a temporary buffer, so overlapping regions are handled. Copying 5 bytes abcde to offset 2 overwrites cdefg, leaving ab + abcde + h. Moving 4 bytes defg to the front overwrites abcd, giving defg + efgh. buf + 6 is "eh", length 2. No NUL is moved; the original terminators at index 8 stay. With memcpy, overlapping source and destination is undefined behaviour. The result depends on the libc implementation, copy direction, CPU and even buffer size: a forward byte copy would produce abababah for the first call, while an optimised copy might happen to work, until a glibc upgrade changes it (this really broke software in 2010). Use memmove whenever regions may overlap, for example shifting data in a receive buffer after consuming a header, or inserting into an array.

title: Main loop and ISRs sharing state
question: Identify every way the main loop and the ISRs can corrupt or miss data here.
answer: 1. No volatile. rx_ready, rx_len and uptime_ms are changed by ISRs, so the optimiser may cache them in registers and the loop never sees new data. 2. Torn 32-bit reads. On a 16-bit CPU uptime_ms is read in two halves. If the timer ISR carries from 0x0000FFFF to 0x00010000 between them, main sees 0x0001FFFF or 0x00000000. Snapshot it with interrupts disabled, or read twice until two reads match. 3. Buffer reused while still being filled. Bytes arriving during handle_line() are appended to the line being parsed; bytes arriving between handle_line() and rx_len = 0 are silently dropped; and rx_len = 0 can race with the ISR's rx_len++. Fix: keep ISRs minimal and push bytes into a single-producer/single-consumer ring buffer (or double-buffer whole lines), mark shared variables volatile, and keep short critical sections for multi-byte state. The unsigned subtraction now - last >= 500 is already wrap-safe.

title: The lost wake-up
question: Explain how the reader can sleep forever even though data arrived, and how wait_event_interruptible() closes the race.
answer: Lost wake-up. The reader checks data_ready (false), and before it gets onto the wait queue, the IRQ fires on another CPU (or preempts it), sets the flag and calls wake_up on an empty queue. The reader then goes to sleep and waits for a wake-up that has already happened. interruptible_sleep_on() was removed in Linux 3.15 because it is inherently racy. wait_event_interruptible(wq, data_ready) runs a loop: prepare_to_wait() adds the task to the queue and sets TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE first, then re-checks the condition, then schedule()s. A wake-up arriving after the check sets the task back to running, so schedule() returns immediately. The condition is re-evaluated after every wake, which also handles spurious wake-ups and multiple readers. Still required: check the return value (-ERESTARTSYS on a signal), and consume data_ready and the data under a spinlock shared with the IRQ, since two readers can both see true. The waker must set the condition before calling wake_up().

title: Reverse the bits of a uint32_t
question: Write rev32(), first the obvious loop, then an O(log n) divide-and-conquer version.
answer: Loop: shift the result left, append the lowest bit of x, shift x right; repeat 32 times. Use an unsigned type so right shifts bring in zeros. Divide and conquer: reversing a word equals swapping its two halves and reversing each half. Do it bottom-up in five steps: swap adjacent bits with mask 0x55555555, then 2-bit pairs (0x33333333), nibbles (0x0F0F0F0F), bytes (0x00FF00FF), and finally the 16-bit halves. That is 5 steps instead of 32 and branch-free. The last two steps are just a byte swap, so __builtin_bswap32() can replace them. Masking before shifting left avoids carrying bits out of the type. Check: rev32(0x12345678) = 0x1E6A2C48, because each nibble is bit-reversed (1 becomes 8, 2 becomes 4, 3 becomes C, ...) and the nibble order is reversed. The kernel provides bitrev32()/bitrev8() (linux/bitrev.h), which ARM64 implements with a single RBIT instruction.

title: skb_push, skb_pull and headroom
question: Explain what skb_push() and skb_pull() do to the sk_buff pointers, and why skb_cow_head() and pskb_may_pull() are needed.
answer: An skb buffer is laid out as head ... data ... tail ... end. Headroom is data - head; len is the packet length. skb_push(skb, n) moves data back by n and adds n to len, returning the new data: you prepend a header with no copy, provided headroom exists. If it does not, skb_push hits skb_under_panic(). skb_pull(skb, n) advances data and subtracts n from len. The bytes are still in the buffer, which is why th remains readable after the pull. skb_cow_head() guarantees enough headroom and that the header area is not shared with a clone, reallocating if necessary, so writing the tag cannot corrupt another user's view. pskb_may_pull() checks the packet has at least TAG_LEN bytes and that they are in the linear area (not in page fragments) before you dereference skb->data. Reload header pointers afterwards; it may reallocate. Drivers create headroom with skb_reserve().

title: A shared interrupt handler
question: This handler shares a level-triggered line with another device. What is wrong with its return values and acknowledgement?
answer: 1. Claims interrupts that are not its own. On a shared line every handler is called for every interrupt. When status == 0 the other device raised it, but this handler still returns IRQ_HANDLED. That defeats the kernel's spurious-interrupt detection, so a stuck line will never be reported or disabled. Start with if (!status) return IRQ_NONE; (and treat 0xffffffff as "device gone or powered off"). 2. Error path returns early without acknowledging. With INT_ERR set it returns IRQ_NONE and never writes INT_CLEAR. A level-triggered line stays asserted, the handler runs again immediately, and after about 100,000 unhandled interrupts the kernel prints irq N: nobody cared and disables the line, taking the other device down with it. Handle the error, clear the status and return IRQ_HANDLED. 3. Use dev_err_ratelimited() in IRQ paths, because an error storm can flood the console and stall the CPU. For heavy work, return IRQ_WAKE_THREAD and use request_threaded_irq().

title: Lock-free SPSC ring buffer
question: Implement rb_push() and rb_pop() without locks or disabling interrupts. Use all RB_SIZE slots.
answer: Use free-running 32-bit indices and mask only when indexing the array. Then head == tail means empty and head - tail == RB_SIZE means full, so all slots are usable with no wasted "gap" slot. Unsigned subtraction stays correct when the counters wrap, as long as RB_SIZE divides 2^32 (a power of two). It is lock-free because each index has a single writer: only the producer stores head and only the consumer stores tail. Ordering is the subtle part: the producer must write the byte before publishing the new head (release), and the consumer must observe head (acquire) before reading the byte. On a single-core MCU volatile indices alone are not enough, because the compiler may move the non-volatile buf store after the head update. On multicore or weakly ordered CPUs you also need hardware barriers, which release/acquire provide. The kernel equivalents are smp_store_release()/smp_load_acquire() (see Documentation/core-api/circular-buffers.rst) and kfifo.
